newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Top prize to South Africa at Geneva inventors show.
newsitem.headline: Top prize to South Africa at Geneva inventors show.

text.p: An inventor from South Africa who designed an industrial device that crushes rocks at mines and quarries in minutes by remote control won the top prize at Geneva's annual inventors' contest on Wednesday.

The jury of the International Exhibition of Inventions said Cape Town inventor John Godsiff, of Swartklip Products company, had been awarded the 1997 Grand Prix for his "revolutionary" design named Ro-Bust.
"Economical and safe, Ro-Bust can break blocks up to ten cubic metres instantly, within three minutes, and then immediately starts the same operation with another rock," the jury's statement said.

The award at the prestigious event, which attracted more than 600 scientists, boffins, engineers and wacky inventors from 44 countries, carries no money. Organisers hope the exhibition will generate new business worth 40 million Swiss francs.
The "Oscar of Inventions" prize, awarded by popular vote among visitors to the exhibition, went to French designer Claude Yviquel for his revolutionary car for the 21st century, OSMOSE.
Light and easily parked, this city car can run with gas, petrol or electricity and adjusts to different energy needs and rules in various countries, according to its creator.
Inventions on display this year included cigarettes that do not produce smoke, solar cookers for refugees, buttons that do not need sewing and a device for women to urinate like men.
A team of Russian rocket scientists, engineers and retired army officers from Moscow's crumbling defence industry, the highlight of this year's event, did not get any prizes.

Russian designs included a night-vision device, a stain-removing "dry cleaning stick" made with rocket fuel technology and a necklace with a crystal pendant that changes color when the sun's ultraviolet rays are dangerous -- made by a factory producing rocket parts for the Russian military industrial complex.
